say.text: A 24-year-old man has had central pain for 18 hours. It has moved to the right iliac fossa (RIF), and he is tender there.
You want his psoas sign. Which manoeuvre do you perform?

choices.label: Internally rotate the flexed right hip, supine
Press firmly over the left iliac fossa, supine
Extend the right hip with him on his left side
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Psoas is a hip flexor, and a retrocaecal appendix lies on top of it. Ask which hip movement loads the muscle, not which one moves the pelvis.
Yes. Extending the right hip stretches the psoas. Pain on that movement suggests a retrocaecal appendix lying on the muscle.
Retrocaecal is the commonest position of the appendix, so this is the sign you will meet most often.
Tempting: internal rotation of the flexed hip is a real right-hip test, and it is easy to file it next to this one.
Nudge: the psoas is a hip flexor. Which of the two movements stretches it?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the psoas again: the sign comes from extending the hip, and the rotation test belongs to another muscle.

say.text: Internal rotation of the flexed right hip stretches obturator internus. That is the obturator sign, and it suggests a pelvic appendix.
The psoas sign is pain on extending the right hip, which suggests a retrocaecal appendix lying on the psoas.
Tempting: pressing the left iliac fossa is the Rovsing manoeuvre, so it feels like the right physical test for this patient.
Nudge: the psoas test does not press anywhere. Which movement of the right hip makes the pain happen?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two: pressing the left side is Rovsing's sign, and it is not a psoas test.

say.text: Pressing the left iliac fossa is Rovsing's sign: pain is felt in the right iliac fossa (K37). It is not a psoas manoeuvre.
The psoas sign is pain on extending the right hip, with the patient on the left side (K38).
Next patient: the examiner flexes the right hip, rotates the leg inwards, and he winces with hypogastric pain.
Name the sign.
Yes. Internal rotation of the flexed right hip stretches obturator internus, and pain there suggests a pelvic appendix touching that muscle.
Tempting: you named the psoas sign first in the last case, and both signs are right-hip movements, so the name comes back easily.
Wrong: the psoas sign is extension of the right hip (K38). Internal rotation of the flexed hip is the obturator sign, for a pelvic appendix (K39).
Tempting: Rovsing's sign is the other right-iliac-fossa sign in the same set, so it can seem to match any hip case.
Wrong: Rovsing's needs pressure in the left iliac fossa and gives right-sided pain (K37). This patient's movement is the obturator sign (K39).
A young man has loin pain on hip extension and little anterior tenderness (K33). The sign and the position both matter.
Which pairing fits the picture?

choices.label: Psoas with pelvic; obturator with retrocaecal
Psoas with retrocaecal; obturator with pelvic
Psoas with retrocaecal; rectal tenderness with retrocaecal
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which organ the appendix touches in each position: the muscle at the back of the abdomen, or the bladder and rectum in the pelvis.
Yes. Each sign follows the organ its position touches: retrocaecal lies on the psoas (K38), pelvic lies on the obturator internus (K39).
Pelvic is the second most common position, after retrocaecal (K93).
Tempting: psoas and pelvic feel like a natural pair, because both are familiar pictures from the exam.
Nudge: which organ does a retrocaecal appendix sit on, and which organ does a pelvic one touch?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so tie each sign to the organ, not to the name: the psoas belongs to the retrocaecal position.

say.text: A retrocaecal appendix lies on the psoas, so extending the hip hurts (K38). It typically gives loin pain (K33).
A pelvic appendix lies against the obturator internus, so internal rotation of the flexed hip hurts (K39).
Tempting: rectal tenderness is a real finding, so it feels as if it could sit with any position of the appendix.
Nudge: right-sided rectal tenderness points to one position. Which one, and where does it sit?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link the rectal sign to where the appendix lies: rectal tenderness comes from the pelvic position.

say.text: Right-sided rectal tenderness suggests a pelvic appendix (K42), so it cannot go with the retrocaecal position.
The correct pairing keeps the psoas with retrocaecal (K38) and the obturator with pelvic (K39).
Why does a pelvic appendix cause diarrhoea, urinary frequency and right rectal tenderness?

choices.label: It lies on the psoas muscle, stretching it
It lies against the rectum and bladder, irritating them
It lies behind the caecum, irritating the ureter

say.text: Yes. A pelvic appendix touches the rectum and bladder, so it causes diarrhoea, frequency and dysuria (K34).
Tempting: the psoas picture is the one you have just learnt, so it sounds like a mechanism for any bowel symptom.
Wrong: stretching the psoas gives pain on hip extension (K38), not bowel symptoms. Right answer: a pelvic appendix touches the rectum and bladder (K34).
Tempting: the ureter is close to the pelvic appendix, so it can seem the nearest structure to irritate.
Wrong: an appendix behind the caecum is retrocaecal, which gives loin pain with little anterior tenderness (K33). Pelvic symptoms come from the rectum and bladder (K34).
Next, Rovsing's sign. Predict first: where is the pressure applied, and where does the patient feel the pain?
Which statement about Rovsing's sign is correct?

choices.label: Pressure in the right iliac fossa causes pain in the left
Pain in the right iliac fossa on extending the right hip
Pressure in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right

say.text: Yes. Pressure in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right iliac fossa. That reversed-looking direction is what makes it Rovsing's sign.
Tempting: the pain is on the right, so pressing the right side feels like the way to reproduce it.
Wrong: the direction runs the other way. Pressure in the left iliac fossa gives pain in the right (K37). Pressing the right side does not test this sign.
Tempting: pain on a right-hip movement is the psoas picture from the first case, so it feels like the same sign.
Wrong: pain on extending the right hip is the psoas sign (K38). Rovsing's is pressure in the left iliac fossa with pain on the right (K37).
Now the Alvarado score, used for a patient with suspected appendicitis. Which items carry 2 points?

choices.label: Migration of pain and rebound tenderness
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Only two items score 2 and the rest score 1. Look for the local sign at the appendix and the one blood result in the score.
Yes. RIF tenderness and leucocytosis each score 2, the other items score 1, and the total is out of 10.
Tempting: migration and rebound are classic appendicitis signs, so they feel like the heavy items in the score.
Nudge: look at the table again. Which two items weigh 2, and do migration and rebound make that list?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the weights: migration and rebound each score 1, and only two items score 2.

say.text: Only tenderness in the right iliac fossa and leucocytosis score 2 (K107). Migration and rebound each score 1.
The total is out of 10, and a score of 7 or more makes appendicitis likely (K46, K47).
Tempting: RIF tenderness and rebound come together on the examination, so the pair feels like one finding.
Nudge: rebound is in the list at a lower weight. Which other item has the same weight as RIF tenderness?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-check the second 2-point item: it is a blood count, not an examination finding.

say.text: Rebound tenderness scores 1, not 2. The two 2-point items are RIF tenderness and leucocytosis (K107).
Your pair keeps the correct examination item but drops the blood count, which also scores 2 (K46).
A patient has migration of pain, nausea, RIF tenderness, rebound tenderness and leucocytosis. What is the Alvarado total?
Yes. Migration 1, nausea 1, RIF tenderness 2, rebound 1 and leucocytosis 2 give 7 (K107, K46).
Tempting: migration and rebound feel like the heavy signs, so giving each 2 seems to follow.
Wrong: migration and rebound each score 1, which gives 7, not 9 (K107). Rebuild the total item by item.
Tempting: leucocytosis is a laboratory result, so it can feel like a minor item scored 1.
Wrong: leucocytosis scores 2 (K107). Scoring it 1 drops the total to 6, and the correct total is 7 (K46).
A young woman has sudden mid-cycle RIF pain. There is no migration, she is afebrile and her count is normal. It settles over a few hours.
Most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Mid-cycle pain with a normal count and no migration does not follow the appendix pattern. Which condition in women causes mid-cycle pain?
Yes. Mittelschmerz is pain from a ruptured Graafian follicle at mid-cycle, a women's cause of RIF pain (K59).
Look-alikes differ by group: children have mesenteric lymphadenitis, women have ectopic pregnancy or mittelschmerz, adults have ureteric colic or caecal diverticulitis (K58, K59, K60).
Tempting: right iliac fossa pain in a young woman is the picture most students learn first, so the diagnosis comes to mind at once.
Nudge: appendicitis is built on its whole pattern. Which feature of this story is missing from that pattern?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember that RIF pain alone never means appendicitis: in a young woman the differential starts with mittelschmerz.

say.text: Mid-cycle RIF pain from a ruptured Graafian follicle, mittelschmerz, mimics appendicitis in a young woman (K59).
RIF pain alone never means appendicitis. Look for the whole pattern, and for the group the patient belongs to (K60).
Pelvic inflammatory disease is a real differential in women (K59), but this story has no fever and a normal count, and the pain settles within hours.
Last check for this segment. Which finding does NOT point to a pelvic appendix?

choices.label: Pain on internal rotation of the flexed right hip
Pain on extension of the right hip

say.text: Yes. Pain on extending the right hip is the psoas sign, which points to a retrocaecal appendix (K38, K21).
Tempting: internal rotation is the other right-hip movement, so it feels like the retrocaecal one.
Wrong: internal rotation of the flexed hip is the obturator sign, which fits a pelvic appendix (K39). The psoas sign is extension (K38).
Tempting: rectal tenderness sounds like a general bowel finding, so it seems to fit any position of the appendix.
Wrong: right-sided rectal tenderness suggests a pelvic appendix touching the rectum (K42). Retrocaecal gives loin pain with little anterior tenderness (K33).
